name: French methodical battle and the Maginot Line (1939-1940)

weightNotes.aggression: Defensive mindset reinforced by the Maginot Line (House ch. 3); the September 1939 Saar offensive advanced a few kilometres and withdrew. Attack only after careful, methodical preparation to minimise casualties (1921 Provisional Instructions, quoted in House ch. 3).
weightNotes.maneuver: Bataille conduite: a tightly controlled set-piece battle where all units advance methodically according to an elaborate plan (House ch. 3; Doughty, Seeds of Disaster). Attrition and firepower, not movement.
weightNotes.flanking: The 1936 regulation's 'defensive without thought of retreat' meant rigid orientation to the front rather than manoeuvring against flank or rear (House ch. 3). The Dyle-Breda advance into Belgium was a forward move into prepared lines, not a flanking manoeuvre.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Doctrine was terrain-oriented: hold and fortify lines (Maginot Line, Dyle line) rather than seek the enemy field army. Middle value because the engine weighs cities against formations, and French objectives were ground, not armies.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Doctrine wanted a large general reserve, but in practice the Breda variant sent Seventh Army, the main reserve, to Holland, the four armoured divisions were scattered behind the front and broken up when committed (House ch. 4). Practice, not paper, sets the weight.
weightNotes.scouting: Air reconnaissance saw the German columns in the Ardennes on 10-12 May but the High Command discounted it; radio use was restricted for fear of signals intelligence (House ch. 3). Low-moderate.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.worldwars high quartile 0.355. Sourced refusal to withdraw: the 1936 regulation's 'defensive without thought of retreat' told units to hold in place (House ch. 3; Doughty). No measured share outside the backtest campaign. Kept under the evidence rule (QA round 4): a standing tactical order to hold in place, not caution about attacking. Weakness: every 1939-1940 French battle that would show it lies inside the France 1940 backtest campaign, so it is not shown in a non-backtest battle.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Doctrine assigned artillery, tanks and aviation to support the infantry, but 36 tank battalions were dispersed among infantry armies without joint training and air support was mostly reconnaissance (House ch. 3-4). Paper combined arms, poor practice.
weightNotes.initiative: Doughty locates the main cause of 1940 in overcentralisation; command moved at First World War pace and radios were to be used only when no other means existed (House ch. 3).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Methodical battle meant no attack before artillery, ammunition and supply were in place; operations never outran supply. Very high.

summary: The French Army of 1939-40 kept the lessons of 1918: firepower kills, so attack only in carefully prepared, centrally controlled set-piece battles where the infantry advances by bounds under massed artillery, with tanks parcelled out in support. The frontier was covered by the Maginot Line, which freed men for a planned advance into Belgium to fight on the Dyle with the British. Command was centralised and slow, radios were distrusted, armoured divisions were few and formed late, and the army was a mobilised militia needing months to train (House ch. 3).
whyItWorked: It won 1918 and it worked where the enemy attacked prepared positions on French terms: the Maginot Line was never broken frontally in May-June 1940, and the Cavalry Corps at Hannut and First Army at Gembloux (12-15 May) stopped German panzer corps in set-piece defence. Its firepower and casualty-saving logic suited a country with a smaller population than Germany.
whereItFailed: Sedan, 13-15 May 1940: the main German mechanised mass came through the Ardennes against two weak reserve divisions at the hinge of the Allied line. The French could not plan and launch counterattacks fast enough (XXI Corps' counterattack of 14 May dissolved into static stop-lines), the general reserve had been sent to Holland, and once panzers were loose in the rear the centrally controlled system could not redeploy in time. France signed an armistice on 22 June 1940, six weeks after the offensive began.
